After impoundment began in Amistad Reservoir on May 31, 1968, the greatest Rio Grande discharge recorded at the gage about 2 miles below Amistad Dam was 62,200 cfs during the flood of September 1974, which had a peak reservoir inflow of 650,000 cfs.
2.17 Historic River Flows. Based upon studies by the US Section, IBWC for the period 1900-1973, the average annual inflow to Amistad Reservoir was 2,194,100 acre feet. From the same study, the maximum and minimum annual inflows to Amistad Reservoir were 5,257,200 acre feet and 629,000 acre feet, respectively, while the maximum and minimum monthly inflows to Amistad Reservoir were 2,964,700 acre feet and 19,000 acre feet, respectively.
2.18 Water Quality. The water quality immediately below Amistad Reservoir is excellent. However, water in the Rio Grande sampled at the US Highway 90 bridge has shown signs of contamination. A Texas Water Quality Board Report has attributed this contamination to probably non-point source loads from the Texas side of the river and/or wastewater discharges from the Mexican side, as evidenced by increases in nitrogen, phosphorus, and suspended solids (TWQB, undated). Eight Mile Creek joins the Rio Grande below Del Rio, and contributes water that is high in total dissolved solids (TDS). There is little difference in test results for chlorides and sulfates on samples taken between Del Rio and Laredo, but total phosphates did increase at Laredo. The data collected by the Texas Water Quality Board indicated that there is not a significant wastewater contamination problem from Del Rio to Laredo.
2.19 Ambient Air Quality. Correspondence with the Texas Air Control Board indicates that Val Verde County should have excellent air quality because it lacks emission sources. Consequently, the area receives low priority in the monitoring program which collects only particulate data. These data indicate low levels of particulates in the Del Rio area except during natural dusty conditions which are typical of arid regions of West Texas. In summary, the area should have low levels of the common pollutants because it lacks emission sources.
2.20 Flora. The limestone hill country around Amistad reflects the change in vegetational types that is characteristic of the historic cattle and drought years of the late 1800's. This area of the southwest that once was covered with chino gramagrass is now replaced by tenacious shrubs and more hardy species of grasses such as slim tridens, fluff grass, and three-awns (Warnoch, 1970). Two vegetational associations are noted by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD, 1976a) on the rolling gravel hills around Amistad Lake. One upland site northeast of the lake is primarily mesquite-huisache-ceniza brush, and the other southeast of the dam is ceniza-guajillo-mesquite-sotol brush. Other similar associations on the hills and rocky slopes along the Rio Grande between Del Rio and Eagle Pass are blackbrush-guajillo-ceniza-mesquite brush, and ceniza-blackbrushcreosotebush. The three most abundant shrubs are blackbrush, ceniza, and guajillo. The Rio Grande floodplain presents contrasting vegetational communities to the upland terrain. Along the river are dense green thickets called "bosques" composed of tall (20-30) ft.) willows, mesquite, salt cedar, giant reed and common reed intermixed with native weeds. Between the river and the rocky slopes is a mixture of salt cedar, mesquite, tree tobacco, lotebush, sugar leaf hackberry, buttonbush, sandgrape, velvet ash, and poison ivy covering thick areas of bermuda, buffle, and johnson grasses.
